source: Ferre (2025) MADIL: An MDL-based Framework for Efficient Program Synthesis in the ARC Benchmark
finding: MADIL writes a program as a pair of grid models. The input model splits the grid into parts (patterns). The output model rebuilds the output from those parts. Learning picks the pair with the shortest two-part code (model plus data given model). No LLM is used.
numbers: Version v3.5 (last ArcPrize 2024 submission), micro-accuracy: 32.1% on 400 public training tasks, about 15.1% on 400 evaluation tasks, 7.0% on the private set. Icecuber (Kaggle 2020): 44.7% train, 30.8% eval, 20.6% private. One CPU thread.
limits: Table 6 text came out scrambled in extraction, so the eval figure is inferred from column order. Author looked only at training tasks when designing, so eval is clean.
agent_relevance: A pure MDL solver is far below LLM systems, so MDL is a selector or prior for our agent, not a replacement for it.

source: Ferre (2025) MADIL: An MDL-based Framework for Efficient Program Synthesis in the ARC Benchmark
finding: The length score finds the right program early. Most solutions come from the first greedy rollout. Search is narrow and deep, not wide and shallow.
numbers: Of 400 eval tasks, 69 had a model correct on all training examples; 57 of those were correct on all test examples (82% generalisation). 54 of 69 solutions came from the first greedy MCTS rollout. Average rank of best model among final models 1.3. 80% of solutions found in the first 20 s of a 180 s budget. Correct models had 3 to 46 nodes, mean 15.2. Only 4 tasks had a solution of size 4 or less.
limits: Eval tasks only. Brute force limited to depth 3 or 4 could not reach models of mean size 15.
agent_relevance: Gives a number for how much a compression score prunes search. Supports using a length score to rank candidate rules in S7.

source: Ferre (2025) MADIL: An MDL-based Framework for Efficient Program Synthesis in the ARC Benchmark
finding: Failure analysis on training tasks where a fitting model was found but failed on test: the main cause is spurious expressions that cancel out a wrong decomposition. Risk rises with fewer training examples and with larger allowed expressions.
numbers: 21 generalisation failures; 62 search failures on tasks that look solvable. Search failure causes: 21 need non-compressive intermediate steps, 15 had top-Kp descriptions not diverse enough, 13 from poor ranking, spurious expressions or slowness.
quote: The major cause is spurious expressions that manage to compensate for the wrong decompositions of grids.
limits: Authors say the contrived expressions should be penalised harder by MDL, so their length model was too lenient. Counts come from training tasks.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for G3: a short fit can still be wrong when the fit contains contrived parts. A length score needs a held-out check and a strict price on complexity.

source: Ferre (2025) MADIL: An MDL-based Framework for Efficient Program Synthesis in the ARC Benchmark
finding: Ablation of MADIL parameters shows what the search needs. Sampling several descriptions per grid matters most. Search beyond greedy helps a little.
numbers: Among 71 eval tasks solved by some v3.2 to v3.6 version: one description sampled (Np=1) loses 19 tasks; Kp=1 loses 6; Np=10 vs 100 loses 1; removing the MCTS parameters loses 3 and 4 tasks; only Np=1 and Se=1 had strong effects.
limits: Task set chosen from already-solved tasks, so it is biased toward easier ones.
agent_relevance: Keeping several candidate readings of the same examples (not just one) was the key ingredient. Matches our S2 idea of holding more than one parse.

source: Ferre (2025) MADIL: An MDL-based Framework for Efficient Program Synthesis in the ARC Benchmark
finding: MADIL and brute-force Icecuber solve overlapping but different tasks. MADIL has clear gaps: no conditionals, no recursion, parses one grid at a time, learns input and output models separately.
numbers: All test outputs correct: MADIL 59 eval tasks, Icecuber 117. Overlap 43, MADIL-only 16.
limits: Icecuber rerun by the author on public sets.
agent_relevance: Complementary solvers: a compression check and a search solver catch different tasks. The listed gaps are a to-do list for any symbolic helper we give the agent.

source: Ferre (2021) First Steps of an Approach to the ARC Challenge based on Descriptive Grid Models and the MDL Principle
finding: First MADIL paper. Models describe grids by a parse tree; learning is a greedy search that shrinks total description length. On the worked task the output grids reached zero residual length.
numbers: 29 of 400 training tasks (7.25%) and 6 of 400 evaluation tasks (1.5%) with a 30 s limit per task. Compression gain 16.3% (six-fold reduction) in the worked example.
limits: Early prototype with a small primitive set. Counts include partial credit.
agent_relevance: Shows the trajectory: 1.5% to about 15% eval over 2021 to 2025 with the same MDL idea. Gains came from more patterns, not from a new principle.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC)
finding: CompressARC treats a puzzle as a code-golf job: find the shortest program that prints all grids, with test outputs left free. It trains a 76K-parameter equivariant network only on the puzzle itself at test time, minimising bits for the latent plus the reconstruction error. No pretraining and no ARC training set.
numbers: 2000 steps per puzzle (about 20 min per puzzle): 20.00% pass@2 on 400 public eval (Table 5; peak 21.5% at 1500 steps), 34.75% pass@2 on 400 training puzzles (Table 4). Eval pass@1 18.5%, pass@1000 33.75%.
quote: solves 20% of evaluation puzzles by minimizing the description length (MDL) of the target puzzle purely during inference time
limits: Heavily hand-engineered architecture; slow (138 h for the whole eval set at 2000 steps on an RTX 4070). Not a language model.
agent_relevance: Strongest evidence that compression of the task alone, at inference time, solves a fifth of ARC-AGI-1 with no pretraining. For an LLM agent the lesson is the objective, not the network.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC)
finding: Baseline comparison under the same data limits: a plain U-Net trained at test time on the demonstration pairs does almost nothing, so the MDL objective and the architecture bias carry the result.
numbers: U-Net baseline 0.75% on public eval versus CompressARC 20%. U-Net with random augmentation was worse than without (training set 1% vs 2.5%). Other Table 1 rows: brute-force rule search 40% on private eval; HRM ablation 31% on public eval; HRM 40.3%; o3 high 87.5% on semi-private.
limits: Row-to-method alignment in Table 1 taken from text order; read with care. Only one baseline architecture.
agent_relevance: A compression objective is not magic by itself; it needs strong built-in symmetries. For us the schema's bias (what counts as simple) matters as much as 'shorter is better'.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC)
finding: Accuracy grows with inference steps and with allowed guesses; the rule is found in stages, first borders, then colours, then the mapping.
limits: The training split was used to design the architecture, so train numbers are optimistic.
agent_relevance: More steps at the compression stage keep paying for a long while; S7 depth should be budgeted, not stopped at the first fit.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC)
finding: Case study: on one puzzle the learned latent shrinks to four information-carrying tensors (a colour-to-direction table and row/column divider positions). When one needed tensor collapsed to zero information the run usually failed.
numbers: One puzzle (272f95fa, Color the Boxes); 14 of 18 tensors fell to zero information.
limits: Single worked example; shows a lucky run.
agent_relevance: Compression finds real rule parts as separate pieces. Failure mode: a needed piece is dropped as too costly. A length score can delete a necessary rule part.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC)
finding: Paper lists limits: no long-range pattern extension, no shape copying (no convolution-like layer), no sharing of compression across puzzles. Joint compression across puzzles was tried and not made to work.
numbers: Capability list in Appendices H and K; no numbers.
limits: Authors report what they tried and failed, with no measured results.
agent_relevance: Names where pure compression stalls: copy-shape and long-range rules. For those the agent should use an explicit tool, not a length prior.

source: Li et al. (2024) Combining Induction and Transduction for Abstract Reasoning
finding: Trained the same LLM family to write a Python program (induction) or to predict the grid directly (transduction). The two solve different tasks even with the same data. Induction wins on precise computation and composing concepts; transduction wins on fuzzy perception.
numbers: 400 public ARC eval tasks, two tries: solved sets overlap little and are stable across random seeds. Best ensemble (induction plus transduction with test-time training and reranking) 56.75%; average human 60.2%, best human 97.8%.
limits: Table text partly scrambled; only the headline 56.75%, 60.2% and 97.8% are certain. Trained on synthetic data grown from 100 seed ARC tasks.
agent_relevance: Program-with-check and direct guess should both be in the loop. A rule-writing path (our S7) is the induction arm; give it a fallback.

source: Li et al. (2024) Combining Induction and Transduction for Abstract Reasoning
finding: Induction scales with sampling budget, and some programs fit all examples but are wrong on test. This is a measured false-positive rate of 'fits every training pair'.
numbers: About 9% of sampled programs that fit the training examples are false positives; about half of that 9% sit in problems where the majority vote still gives the right answer. Solve rate rises almost monotonically from 0 to 2000 samples.
quote: about 9% of samples that fit the training examples are false-positives
limits: Measured for their fine-tuned induction model, not frontier LLMs.
agent_relevance: A fit on the examples is not proof: about 1 in 11 fitting programs failed on test. Use majority vote or a length preference among fitting candidates (G3).

source: Li et al. (2024) Combining Induction and Transduction for Abstract Reasoning
finding: Simple ensembling rule: try induction first, and fall back to transduction when no program fits all examples.
numbers: Reported ensemble rows include 26.50% (induction 18.78% at 2048 samples, transduction 15.25% at beam 20) in a GPT-4o-mini description-and-code setup.
limits: Row labels scrambled in extraction; the pairing of numbers with setups is uncertain.
agent_relevance: A plain 'rule first, guess second' order captured most of the gain without a learned router.

source: Akyurek et al. (2025) The Surprising Effectiveness of Test-Time Training for Few-Shot Learning
finding: Test-time training (fine-tune on augmented copies of the task's own examples, then vote across augmentations) sharply lifts a neural solver. Adding the BARC program synthesizer lifts it more.
numbers: ARC public validation, pass@2: fine-tuned baseline 18.3%, with TTT 47.1%; on BARC base 53.0%; ensemble with BARC synthesizer 61.9% (average human 60.2%). Removing geometric transformations drops 16 of 29 ablation tasks (55%); hierarchical voting approaches the oracle choice.
limits: Needs gradient updates per task, so it does not carry over to a prompt-only agent. Without the BARC models their own system scores lower.
agent_relevance: Voting across re-posed versions of a puzzle is the cheap part a prompt-only agent can copy. The program synthesizer adds on top of TTT.

source: Franzen et al. (2025) Product of Experts with LLMs: Boosting Performance on ARC Is a Matter of Perspective
finding: Candidate answers are scored by their total log-probability across several augmented views of the task (product of experts). This works like a code-length selector: lower summed negative log-probability means a shorter code under the model. It cut false positives.
numbers: Public ARC eval, two guesses, NeMo-Minitron-8B: baseline 18.3%; + test-time training 44.5%; + 16 augmented samples 62.5%; + product-of-experts selection 67.6%; + depth-first sampling 71.6% (286.5 of 400). Llama-3.2-3B: 14.9%, 40.9%, 52.9%, 59.5%, 61.4%. About 2 cents per task.
limits: Open model fine-tuned on ARC-like data, not zero-shot. One benchmark split.
agent_relevance: The selection gain (about 5 points) came from a likelihood-as-length score across views, not from more sampling. The same idea can pick among rival rules in S7.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Hypothesis Search: Inductive Reasoning with Language Models
finding: GPT-4 proposes abstract natural-language hypotheses, turns each into a Python program, and checks programs on the training pairs. Going through hypotheses first beat writing programs directly.
numbers: 100-task ARC subset: direct prompting 17%; automated pipeline with LLM-summarised hypotheses 30%; human picks from LLM candidates 33%; human-written hypotheses up to 45% with 3 feedback rounds. Chain of thought without programs 19%. 1D-ARC: direct 39.6%, program-only 61.1%, full 73.1%. Execution feedback on summarised hypotheses: 24, 28, 28, 30% for 0 to 3 rounds.
limits: Random 100-task ARC subset; GPT-4 only.
agent_relevance: Shows that natural-language hypothesis first, code second, verify by running, works as an S2 to S7 chain. A shortlist step (summarise or pick) matters because it limits search.

source: Butt et al. (2024) CodeIt: Self-Improving Language Models with Prioritized Hindsight Replay
finding: A language model samples programs in a DSL, relabels failed programs with the output they actually produced (hindsight), and trains on that. Over time it finds shorter programs.
numbers: Solves 15% of ARC evaluation tasks, above earlier symbolic work including Ferre 2021 and GPT-4 prompting (12% in Gendron et al.). In later iterations it found a shorter program for 53% of solved tasks. Fails on solutions longer than 11 lines.
quote: producing a shorter solution in a later meta-iteration
limits: Needs a hand-built DSL and training; small CodeT5 model.
agent_relevance: Shorter-program refinement happened without an explicit MDL term, from replay. Program length is a signal the agent can use when it revisits a solved task.

source: Ouellette (2024) Towards Efficient Neurally-Guided Program Induction for ARC-AGI
finding: Compared three ways to guide search over DSL programs. Best was learning a probability model over programs and enumerating in probability order (GridCoder). This is a learned prior, the nearest competitor to an MDL prior.
numbers: Eval set at 15-minute budget: GridCoder 5.75%, conditional variant 5.5%, MCTS+LVM 3.25%, pixelwise-similarity 2.75%, learned-similarity 1%. On the 29 tasks solvable in the DSL (7.25% of eval): 79.3% for GridCoder. DSL versions 1 to 3 eval 5.75%, 7.75%, 8.25%; hidden test 0%, 1%, 1%.
limits: Tiny absolute scores; the DSL coverage ceiling is the limit. Out-of-distribution transfer was weak.
agent_relevance: Both MDL and learned-prior search sit below the DSL coverage ceiling. Missing primitives are a bigger problem than the search.

source: Xu, Khalil, Sanner (2023) Graphs, Constraints, and Search for the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARGA)
finding: ARGA searches over object graphs with constraint acquisition, state hashing and tabu search, using a short object-centric DSL. It is a non-MDL symbolic route evaluated on 160 object-centric tasks.
numbers: ARGA solves 63 of 160 (39.38%) with 57 correct on test (35.62%); ablations remove one component each and solve 60 to 64 of 160. A comparison block on the same slice shows 79 of 160 (49.38%) with 64 correct on test (40.00%) but its label was lost in extraction.
limits: Comparator label scrambled; subset of 160 tasks, not the full set.
agent_relevance: A short object-first vocabulary does well on object tasks without any compression score.

source: Johnson, Vong, Lake, Gureckis (2021) Fast and flexible: Human program induction in abstract reasoning tasks
finding: Humans solve most ARC tasks, and tasks whose rule people described with longer text were solved less often: a small human sign of the simplicity idea.
numbers: 95 MTurk participants, 40 training tasks, about 23.5 participants per task. Average accuracy 83.8% per task (SD 16.7%) within three attempts; 65% of tasks at 80% or more; hardest task 38.1%. Mean description 20 words (SD 5). Mixed model: description length b = -0.17, 95% CI [-0.315, -0.020], p = 0.03. Kaggle winner solved 57.5% of the same 40 tasks; Spearman with humans 0.35.
limits: Descriptions were written after the attempt, so length may follow difficulty and not cause it. Training tasks only.
agent_relevance: A weak link between short rule wording and being right. 'Does the rule fit in a sentence' is a cheap sanity check for the agent.

source: LeGris, Vong, Lake, Gureckis (2024) H-ARC: A Robust Estimate of Human Performance on the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus Benchmark
finding: Large human baseline on all 800 public tasks. It is lower than the earlier 83.8% from a 40-task sample.
numbers: 784 participants on training tasks, 948 on evaluation tasks. Average task accuracy after 3 attempts: 76.2% training (CI 73.3 to 77.2), 64.2% evaluation (CI 55.9 to 68.9); after 2 attempts 72.6% and 60.2%; after 1 attempt 59.9% and 47.8%. Best-case coverage 98.8% on both sets. 5 training and 5 evaluation tasks solved by nobody.
limits: Online workers; 10.3% of task data missing from dropout, handled by imputation bounds.
agent_relevance: Use 60.2% on eval with two tries as the human reference for any ARC result of our agent, not 80%.

source: Pinkard et al. (2026) ARC-AGI-2: A New Challenge for Frontier AI Reasoning Systems
finding: The new benchmark was built to defeat brute force and memorisation. Search-over-DSL scores collapse while humans stay high.
numbers: Semi-private ARC-AGI-1 vs ARC-AGI-2 (May 2025): Icecuber 17.0% vs 1.6%; o3 (medium) 53.0% vs 3.0%; ARChitects 56.0% vs 2.5%; o4-mini 41.8% vs 2.4%; o1-pro 23.3% vs 0.9%; Claude 3.7 (8K) 21.2% vs 0.9%. Humans: every ARC-AGI-2 task solved by at least two non-experts; 66% of attempted test pairs solved; 75% of attempts per task.
limits: Authors treat ARC-AGI-2 scores under 5% as noise. The author line on the arXiv file differs from the ARC Prize team; cite with care.
agent_relevance: Anything tuned to ARC-AGI-1 style (MDL over a DSL, brute force) must be rechecked on ARC-AGI-2; the ARC-1 numbers do not carry over.

source: Jolicoeur-Martineau (2025) Less is More: Recursive Reasoning with Tiny Networks
finding: A tiny recursive network trained on ARC data gets strong scores, a contrast to MDL-only methods that use no task data.
numbers: 45% on ARC-AGI-1 and 8% on ARC-AGI-2 test accuracy with under 0.01% of the parameters of the large LLMs it is compared to; Gemini 2.5 Pro 4.9% on ARC-AGI-2 in its text.
limits: Only the abstract and introduction read. Uses ARC-style training data with augmentation.
agent_relevance: Contrast case: much better than CompressARC's 20% but it uses training data. The no-training MDL result is a different point on the data-cost curve.

source: Cole and Osman (2025) Don't Throw the Baby Out with the Bathwater: How and Why Deep Learning for ARC
finding: Test-time fine-tuning and Augment-Inference-Reverse-Augmentation-and-Vote (AIRV) are the main methods of the MindsAI line; the paper argues for the deep-learning route over program synthesis.
numbers: Abstract-level: AIRV alone gives up to 260% relative improvement (base model, fully trained) and test-time fine-tuning a further 300%.
limits: Relative gains, not absolute scores; only abstract and a few lines read. Authors are a competing team, so it is argument as well as measurement.
agent_relevance: Voting over reversed augmentations is the transferable piece (matches Franzen and Akyurek). No MDL term in the method.

source: Macfarlane and Bonnet (2024) Searching Latent Program Spaces
finding: Latent program network: an encoder maps examples to a latent code, and gradient search in that latent space at test time refines it. A compression-flavoured search done in a learned space.
numbers: Pattern-task accuracy 67.5% with no test-time gradient steps and higher with steps; an ARC-AGI eval ablation row climbs from 9.10% to 15.50% as samples grow.
limits: Only grep lines read; the ARC ablation row is not tied to a clear set. Low weight.
agent_relevance: Another route to 'find the simplest latent explanation at test time'; weaker than CompressARC on ARC.

source: Hodel (2024) Addressing the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus via Procedural Example Generation (re-arc)
finding: Hand-built a generator for each of the 400 training tasks so any number of new examples can be sampled. It is the data source behind many neural ARC systems, including the BARC and test-time-training work above.
numbers: 400 generators, one per training task. Hodel's ARCathon 2022 DSL search scored 6% on the private set (CodeIt Table).
limits: No accuracy numbers in the paper; only the abstract and a few lines read.
agent_relevance: Strong neural systems still lean on task-specific generators, which MDL-only systems avoid.
